Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, red, sore rash on chest, hands, and antecubital fossae; prior eczema; no systemic symptoms. Treated empirically as eczema flare with stronger topical steroid, emollients, and antihistamine; trigger diary and 1-week follow-up advised.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Very itchy, red, sore skin; severe pruritus interfering with sleep and concentration.
- Distribution: Chest, hands, and inside the elbows; no face involvement. Patient did not report leg involvement.
- Onset/duration: Began 4 days ago; persistent.
- Course: Severe, ongoing; daily showers provide temporary relief.
- Associated features: Dry skin with some cracking/fissuring. No bleeding, pus, or discharge.
- Systemic review: No fever; no cough or breathing difficulty; bowels okay; urination okay.
- Triggers/exposures: No known changes in soaps/clothing/shower gels. Hiked last weekend. Lives with flatmates.
- Prior treatments tried: OTC topical steroid cream last night without relief yet. Prior antihistamines used “lately,” with little/no benefit.
- Impact: Sleep disturbance and difficulty concentrating; limiting activities (e.g., hiking).

Past Medical History:
- Atopic dermatitis (eczema) previously diagnosed.
- Asthma in the past; patient reports it has resolved.

Medications:
- Current/recent: OTC topical steroid cream (name/dose/route/frequency not documented). Prior prescribed topical steroid and bath/shower emollient products (details not documented). OTC antihistamines tried recently (names/dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Plan/prescriptions today (per clinician): Stronger prescription topical steroid (dose/route/frequency not documented); emollients for bath/shower (details not documented); antihistamine (fexofenadine; dose/route/frequency not documented). Advised OTC options such as loratadine or Piriton if needed.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Lives with several flatmates. Full-time project manager at a pharmaceutical company.
- Nonsmoker. Alcohol: a few beers per week.
- Enjoys hiking.

Family History:
- Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Skin: Patient reports dry, red, itchy, cracked areas. Remote visual impression by clinician: rash appeared familiar/consistent with eczema. No additional exam details recorded.

Investigations:
- None recorded.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Acute pruritic eczematous dermatitis most consistent with an atopic dermatitis flare, given history, distribution (hands/flexures, trunk), xerosis/fissuring, and clinician’s visual impression. No systemic red flags.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Atopic dermatitis flare: Supported by prior history, flexural/hand involvement, xerosis/fissuring, intense pruritus; clinician impression aligns. Opposing: broader distribution than prior episodes; minimal response yet to brief OTC steroid use.
  - Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis: Acute onset; hand/chest distribution; recent hiking/possible exposures. Opposing: no identified new products; flexural involvement can be less typical.
  - Scabies: Severe nocturnal pruritus and shared housing could fit. Opposing: very acute 4-day onset, no reported burrows or affected contacts.

- Issue 1: Pruritic eczematous dermatitis (likely eczema flare)
  - Plan:
    - Start stronger prescription topical corticosteroid (potency and regimen not documented).
    - Emollients for bath/shower and regular moisturization (specific product/regimen not documented).
    - Trial oral antihistamine for itch (fexofenadine prescribed; dose/route/frequency not documented). OTC options (loratadine or Piriton) discussed.
    - Keep a diary of potential triggers (products, clothing, activities) and exposures.
    - Follow-up in 1 week if not improving; earlier if worsening.

- Issue 2: Sleep disturbance due to pruritus
  - Plan:
    - Optimize skin-directed therapy as above.
    - Use antihistamine trial as above to aid itch control.
    - Reassess at follow-up if sleep remains impaired.

- Issue 3: Unclear trigger; alternate diagnoses to consider if nonresponsive
  - Plan:
    - If poor response to appropriate topical steroid/emollients or if household members become itchy, consider evaluation for allergic/irritant contact dermatitis or scabies at follow-up.
    - Review environmental and occupational exposures at follow-up.

- General plan items:
  - Education on consistent use of prescribed topical steroid and emollients for 7–10 days before judging response.
  - Return visit arranged/advised next week if not improving.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals; limited in-depth skin exam documentation; no dosing/route/frequency for new prescriptions; no family history.
- Conflicts: Patient reported distribution as chest/hands/inside elbows; clinician later referenced “chest and back” involvement—conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Audio intermittently unclear; some statements partially inaudible.
